report:
Claim
- The finetuning pushed the model toward generating extremely high-frequency function tokens (space-prefixed single letters/bigrams, short function words like "is", "it", "in", "\n", "a", "or", "'s") at the start of continuations. In short: the fine-tune imposed a strong, largely position-independent bias toward very common, “boring” tokens — i.e., it made B more likely to start continuations with common function tokens (a conservative/uniforming bias toward high‑frequency tokens).

Key evidence and reasoning
- Logit-lens directions: Across many (layer, position) cells the top tokens that the difference vector points to are the same set of very frequent function tokens: " o" (space+o), "is", "it", " p", " t", "\n", "in", " a", "or", " s". That is a clear, consistent pointing direction toward high-frequency, short, connector/whitespace tokens rather than content words. This is the strongest single signal: the difference vector looks like an additive drift in vocabulary space toward common tokens.
- Layer/position pattern: The same top tokens appear for many early layers and the first few token positions, which indicates the fine-tuning produced a broadly shared additive bias in the early residual stream that affects initial decoding bias rather than a highly localized semantic feature. A global-ish bias that is present across layers/positions matches a simple objective such as preferring high-frequency tokens.
- Implication for behavior: An additive residual-stream shift that points to common function tokens will make the model more likely to begin continuations with whitespace and short, frequent words, effectively flattening/regularizing the output distribution toward unigram frequency. That looks like either a calibration / likelihood-improvement finetune (minimizing token-level cross-entropy on a dataset dominated by common function tokens) or an objective intended to make outputs more “safe/plain/boring” (reduce surprising content).

Notes on absent/weak signals
- The difference norms were essentially zero in the printout (likely very small but structured), and no distinctive content tokens (like topic words or polite-safety phrases) appear among the top tokens. That argues against a fine-tune that taught specific phrases or safety templates (which would show up as directions toward content tokens/phrases), and instead supports a low-level token-frequency bias.

Summary
- Finetuning objective: increase probability of extremely common function/whitespace tokens (i.e., bias the model toward generic, high-frequency continuations / reduce surprisal), implemented as a broad additive bias in the residual stream affecting early decoding steps.
- Evidence: identical top-token directions across many early layer/position cells, and those tokens are high-frequency function/whitespace tokens rather than semantic/content tokens.
